lexemes.note: Followed by לְ: מִתַּחַת לַשֻּׁלְחָן “under the table”. With pronouns: מִתַּחְתַּי, מִתַּחְתֶּיךָ …

profile.feeling: Lost keys under the sofa, the cat under the bed.

examples.tr: The key is under the sofa.
The bag is under the table.
The dog sleeps under the bed.

synonyms.nuance: “under” without לְ, in formal and written style: תַּחַת הַשֻּׁלְחָן; it also means “instead of”

etymology.text: מִן “from” + תַּחַת “under”; תַּחַת is related to Arabic تَحْتَ (taḥta), Ge’ez taḥtä and Ugaritic tḥt (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic تَحْتَ (taḥta) “under” is the same word as תַּחַת (Wiktionary).
As in English, מִתַּחַת לַשֻּׁלְחָן also means “under the table”: secretly, illegally.
pitfalls: Say מִתַּחַת לְ… with לְ: מִתַּחַת לַשֻּׁלְחָן — not *מִתַּחַת הַשֻּׁלְחָן.
The לְ fuses with the article: לְ + הַשֻּׁלְחָן → לַשֻּׁלְחָן.
subtleties: “Downstairs, below” without a noun is לְמַטָּה: הוּא לְמַטָּה “he is downstairs”.

profile.feeling: Right beside: the lamp next to the bed, the bank next to the post office.

examples.tr: The lamp is next to the bed.
The bank is next to the post office.
He lives by the sea.

synonyms.nuance: “close to, adjacent to” — formal, in addresses and notices

etymology.text: From לְ “to” + יַד “hand of”: roughly “at the hand of” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: It is literally “at the hand of” — as English says “close at hand”.
pitfalls: No לְ after it: לְיַד הַבַּיִת, not *לְיַד לַבַּיִת.
With pronouns the vowel changes: לְיָדִי, לְיָדְךָ, לְיָדָהּ (Wiktionary).
subtleties: לְיַד is right beside; קָרוֹב לְ… is “near”, possibly farther away.

lexemes.note: “in front of” (place); the same word is “before” in time (lesson 15) and “ago”: לִפְנֵי שָׁנָה “a year ago”.

profile.feeling: In front: the table before the sofa, the bus in front of the house.

examples.tr: The table is in front of the sofa.
The bus is standing in front of the house.
before dinner
Before work I (m.) drink coffee.

examples.text: הוּא חוֹזֵר הַבַּיְתָה לִפְנֵי אֲרוּחַת הָעֶרֶב.
examples.tr: He comes home before dinner.
He was here a year ago.

etymology.text: לְ “to, for” + פְּנֵי “face of”, the construct form of פָּנִים “face” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: German vor works the same way: vor dem Haus “in front of the house”, vor einem Jahr “a year ago”.
pitfalls: The same word is “before” in time (lesson 15) and “ago”: לִפְנֵי שָׁנָה “a year ago”.
“Opposite, facing” is מוּל, not לִפְנֵי.
subtleties: With pronouns: לְפָנַי “in front of me”, לְפָנֶיךָ, לְפָנָיו (Wiktionary).

profile.feeling: Out of sight: behind the door, behind the house.

examples.tr: The garden is behind the house.
The bag is behind the door.
What is behind the wall?

phrases.meaning: behind the scenes, out of public view

synonyms.nuance: “at the back, behind” without a noun: הוּא יוֹשֵׁב מֵאָחוֹר

etymology.text: מִן “from” + אֲחוֹרֵי, the construct form of אָחוֹר “back” (Wiktionary gives no etymology of its own).

funFacts: Hebrew likes מִ “from” in place words: מִתַּחַת, מֵאֲחוֹרֵי, מִשְּׂמֹאל — as if seen “from” there.
pitfalls: אַחֲרֵי is “after” (in time): אַחֲרֵי הָאֲרוּחָה. For a place say מֵאֲחוֹרֵי.
Without a noun use מֵאָחוֹר “at the back”.
subtleties: With pronouns: מֵאֲחוֹרַי “behind me”, מֵאֲחוֹרֶיךָ (Wiktionary).

lexemes.note: Between X and Y: בֵּין X לְY (standard) or בֵּין X וּבֵין Y; in speech also בֵּין X וְY.

profile.feeling: In the middle: between the sofa and the window.

examples.tr: The table is between the sofa and the window.
The bank is between the post office and the supermarket.
This stays between friends.

etymology.text: Compare Arabic بَيْنَ (bayna) and Aramaic byn (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic بَيْنَ (bayna) is the same word; “international” is בֵּינְלְאֻמִּי, “between nations”.
pitfalls: The second item takes לְ (standard: בֵּין הַבַּיִת לַגִּנָּה) or וּבֵין; plain וְ is heard in speech.
לְ fuses with the article: לַחַלּוֹן, לַסּוּפֶּר.
subtleties: With pronouns: בֵּינִי לְבֵינְךָ “between you and me” (a fixed phrase).

lexemes.note: An adjective: it agrees with its noun (הַשּׁוּק קָרוֹב, הַתַּחֲנָה קְרוֹבָה). “Near to” takes לְ: קָרוֹב לַבַּיִת. As an adverb it stays קָרוֹב: הוּא גָּר קָרוֹב.

profile.feeling: Just round the corner — five minutes on foot.

examples.tr: The supermarket is close.
The stop is close to the house.
He is a close friend.

etymology.text: From the same root as Arabic قَرِيب (qarīb) “close, near” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic قَرِيب (qarīb) is the same word; Turkish akraba “relatives” comes from its Arabic plural أَقْرِبَاء.
pitfalls: It agrees: קָרוֹב, קְרוֹבָה, קְרוֹבִים, קְרוֹבוֹת — הַתַּחֲנָה קְרוֹבָה.
“Near to” takes לְ: קָרוֹב לַבַּיִת (but “far from” takes מִ).
subtleties: As an adverb it does not change: הִיא גָּרָה קָרוֹב “she lives nearby”.
בְּקָרוֹב “soon” is “in the near (time)”.

lexemes.note: An adjective: it agrees with its noun (שְׂדֵה הַתְּעוּפָה רָחוֹק, הָאוּנִיבֶרְסִיטָה רְחוֹקָה). “Far from” takes מִ: רָחוֹק מִכָּאן.

profile.feeling: A long way off — a long bus ride away.

examples.tr: The airport is far.
The university is far from here.
They live far away.
He is a distant relative.

etymology.text: Cognate with Tigre rəḥux̣ and Dahalik ruḥuq “far” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew pairs the prepositions like English: רָחוֹק מִ… “far from”, קָרוֹב לְ… “close to”.
pitfalls: “Far from” takes מִ: רָחוֹק מִכָּאן, רָחוֹק מֵהָעִיר.
It agrees: רָחוֹק, רְחוֹקָה, רְחוֹקִים, רְחוֹקוֹת.
subtleties: As an adverb it does not change: הֵם גָּרִים רָחוֹק “they live far away”.

profile.feeling: Indoors, in the warm.

examples.tr: Dad is inside.
What is inside?
The children are inside, in the house.

etymology.text: From בְּ “in” + פְּנִים, from פָּנִים “face; interior” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The Ministry of the Interior is מִשְׂרַד הַפְּנִים, “the ministry of the inside”.
pitfalls: Where? בִּפְנִים. Where to? פְּנִימָה: בּוֹא פְּנִימָה “come in”.
With a noun say בְּ… or בְּתוֹךְ…: בַּבַּיִת / בְּתוֹךְ הַבַּיִת.
subtleties: פָּנִים is both “face” and “inside”.

profile.feeling: Out in the open: the garden, the street, the weather.

examples.tr: The children are outside.
It is cold outside.
We are eating outside.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; the direction “out” is הַחוּצָה.

etymology.text: From בְּ “in” + הַ “the” + חוּץ “outside” (Wiktionary): “in the outside”.

funFacts: Abroad is חוּץ לָאָרֶץ, “outside the Land”, shortened to חוּ״ל.
pitfalls: Where? בַּחוּץ. Where to? הַחוּצָה: צֵא הַחוּצָה “go out”.
חוּץ מִ… means “except”: כֻּלָּם חוּץ מִמֶּנִּי “everyone except me”.
subtleties: It already contains the article: בַּ = בְּ + הַ (Wiktionary).

lexemes.note: “On the left” = מִשְּׂמֹאל (מִ doubles the שׂ); “to the left” = שְׂמֹאלָה.

override.N;SG;INDF;PFX: the form after the prefix מִ, whose נ doubles the first letter (מִשְּׂמֹאל); Wiktionary lists only the plain form.

profile.feeling: Directions: the kitchen is on the left.

examples.tr: The kitchen is on the left.
The bank is to the left of the post office.
the left hand
He is a left-winger (“a man of the Left”).

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *śimaʔl-, cognate with Arabic شِمَال (šimāl), Akkadian šumēlum and Aramaic סְמָלָא; the sense “north” comes from facing the sunrise, with the north on the left (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic شِمَال (šimāl) means both “left” and “north” — Hebrew שְׂמֹאל once did too (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: “On the left” is מִשְּׂמֹאל (with a doubled שׂ); “to the left” is שְׂמֹאלָה.
The ש is a שׂ (s): smol.
subtleties: Facing the sunrise, left is north: Biblical שְׂמֹאל can mean “north” (Wiktionary).
The adjective is שְׂמָאלִי “left, left-wing”.

lexemes.note: “On the right” = מִיָּמִין (מִ doubles the י); “to the right” = יָמִינָה.

override.N;SG;INDF;PFX: the form after the prefix מִ, whose נ doubles the first letter (מִיָּמִין); Wiktionary lists only the plain form.

profile.feeling: Directions: the bathroom is on the right.

senses.def: right (the right side or direction); the right hand

examples.tr: The bathroom is on the right.
The supermarket is to the right of the bank.
He is the manager’s right hand.
a right-wing party

collocations.tr: the right hand; a right-hand man

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *yamīn-, from Proto-Afroasiatic *yamin- (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Binyamin (בִּנְיָמִין, Benjamin) is “son of the right hand”.
pitfalls: “On the right” is מִיָּמִין (with a doubled י); “to the right” is יָמִינָה.
Feminine (Wiktionary), unlike שְׂמֹאל.
subtleties: Facing the sunrise, right is south: Biblical יָמִין can mean “south” (Wiktionary) — and תֵּימָן, Yemen, is “the south”.
The adjective is יְמָנִי “right, right-wing”.

override.N;SG;DEF;PFX: the definite form after the fused prepositions בַּ / לַ (בְּ / לְ + הַ), which drop the ה of the article: הַמִּטְבָּח → (בַּ / לַ)מִּטְבָּח; Wiktionary lists only the full definite form הַמִּטְבָּח.

profile.feeling: The smell of cooking, the heart of the family flat.

examples.tr: Mum is in the kitchen.
The kitchen is small but comfortable.
I (m.) love Greek cuisine.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; a kitchenette is a מִטְבָּחוֹן.

etymology.text: From the root of טַבָּח “cook” and טָבַח “to slaughter”; cognate with Arabic مَطْبَخ (maṭbaḵ) “kitchen” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Turkish mutfak “kitchen” comes from Arabic مَطْبَخ (maṭbaḵ) — the same word as מִטְבָּח.
pitfalls: With the article the מ doubles: הַמִּטְבָּח; “in the kitchen” = בַּמִּטְבָּח.
Before another noun: מִטְבַּח־.
subtleties: A kosher kitchen keeps two sets of dishes, for meat and for milk.

profile.feeling: Shower, bathtub, towels — and a queue in the morning.

examples.tr: The bathroom is on the right.
The flat has two bathrooms.
The bathroom is small.

synonyms.nuance: in speech often just “the bath”: הוּא בָּאַמְבַּטְיָה (Wiktionary lists “bathroom” as a sense)

etymology.text: From חֲדַר־ “room (of)” + אַמְבַּטְיָה “bathtub” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: אַמְבַּטְיָה is the bathtub itself; the room is “the room of the bathtub”.
pitfalls: Masculine, because of חֶדֶר: חֲדַר אַמְבַּטְיָה גָּדוֹל (אַמְבַּטְיָה alone is feminine).
The article goes on the second word: חֲדַר הָאַמְבַּטְיָה.
subtleties: In Israeli flats the toilet is often a separate small room, the שֵׁרוּתִים.

profile.feeling: Quiet, a bed and a wardrobe — the room for sleep.

examples.tr: The children are in the bedroom.
We have three bedrooms.
My bedroom is small.

synonyms.nuance: the parents’ bedroom, the master bedroom

etymology.text: From חֲדַר־ “room (of)” + שֵׁנָה “sleep” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: German Schlafzimmer is built the same way: “room of sleep”.
pitfalls: “In the bedroom” is בַּחֲדַר הַשֵּׁנָה: בְּ before the hataf patah of חֲדַר becomes בַּ, and the article goes on שֵׁנָה.
subtleties: Israeli flats are counted in rooms: a דִּירַת שָׁלוֹשׁ חֲדָרִים has a living room and two bedrooms.

profile.feeling: The sofa, the television, guests on a Friday evening.

examples.tr: The phone is in the living room.
We are sitting in the living room.
We bought a new living-room set.

synonyms.nuance: “living room” in ads and on plans

etymology.text: An internationalism, from French salon (Wiktionary).

funFacts: German Salon, Greek σαλόνι, Russian салон, Turkish salon — all from French salon.
pitfalls: With the article the ס doubles: הַסָּלוֹן; “in the living room” = בַּסָּלוֹן.
A hairdresser’s is a מִסְפָּרָה, not a סָלוֹן.
subtleties: In Israel the סָלוֹן is the main room of the flat, where guests are received.

profile.feeling: Lemon trees, herbs and children on the grass.

senses.def: a small park, a public garden

examples.tr: The children are in the garden.
We have a small garden.
The public garden is next to the house.

synonyms.nuance: a garden, a park (גַּן לְאֻמִּי); also a kindergarten

etymology.text: The feminine counterpart of גַּן “garden” (Song of Songs 6:11 אֶל גִּנַּת אֱגוֹז); גַּן comes from Proto-Semitic *g-n-n “to protect” and is cognate with Arabic جَنَّة (janna) (Wiktionary, under גַּן).

funFacts: The Garden of Eden is גַּן עֵדֶן; Arabic جَنَّة “paradise” is the same root (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: Written גינה in full spelling; plural גִּנּוֹת.
“In the garden” = בַּגִּנָּה.
subtleties: גַּן alone is often a kindergarten: הַיֶּלֶד בַּגַּן “the child is at kindergarten”.

profile.feeling: Cool stone tiles under bare feet.

examples.tr: The bag is on the floor.
The floor is clean.
The children are sitting on the floor.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; a storey is a קוֹמָה.

etymology.text: Wiktionary gives no etymology. A Biblical word for a paved floor (רִצְפַת בַּהַט וָשֵׁשׁ, Esther 1:6), from the root ר־צ־ף “to pave, to lay in a row”.

funFacts: The same root gives רֶצֶף “sequence” and רְצִיפוּת “continuity” — tiles laid in an unbroken row.
pitfalls: A floor of a building (a storey) is קוֹמָה, not רִצְפָּה.
With the article: הָרִצְפָּה (qamats: ר never doubles).
subtleties: Israeli tiled floors are washed with lots of water and a squeegee — the סְפּוֹנְגָ׳ה.

profile.feeling: Four floors and no lift.

examples.tr: The stairs are on the left.
The children are sitting on the stairs.
There is no lift, only stairs.

etymology.text: The plural of מַדְרֵגָה “step” (Wiktionary), from the root ד־ר־ג (Biblical בְּסֵתֶר הַמַּדְרֵגָה, Song of Songs 2:14).

funFacts: The root ד־ר־ג also gives דַּרְגָּה “rank, level” — going up step by step.
pitfalls: One step is מַדְרֵגָה; “stairs” is the plural מַדְרֵגוֹת, and it is feminine.
With the article the מ doubles: הַמַּדְרֵגוֹת.
subtleties: חֲדַר הַמַּדְרֵגוֹת is the shared stairwell of a block of flats.

profile.feeling: Books, jars and plants on the shelf.

examples.tr: The books are on the shelf.
The glass is on the shelf.
There are shelves in the kitchen.

synonyms.nuance: a bookcase, a set of shelves

etymology.text: Wiktionary gives no etymology; it has the noun pattern מַקְטָל (Wiktionary).

funFacts: It also names the flap on an aircraft wing (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: The ד is doubled: ma-DAF; with the article: הַמַּדָּף.
On the shelf = עַל הַמַּדָּף (on), not בַּמַּדָּף.
subtleties: In shops, עַל הַמַּדָּפִים means “in the shops, on sale”.

profile.feeling: An afternoon nap in front of the television.

examples.tr: The key is under the sofa.
Dad is sleeping on the sofa.
We have a new sofa in the living room.

etymology.text: Compare Arabic صُفَّة (ṣuffa) “sofa, long seat of stone or brick”, from Aramaic צפא “mat”; the word may have entered European languages via Turkish or through Moorish Spain (Wiktionary).

funFacts: English and German Sofa came, via Turkish, from Arabic ṣuffa (Wiktionary) — a cousin of סַפָּה.
pitfalls: Feminine: סַפָּה נוֹחָה.
With the article the ס doubles: הַסַּפָּה.
subtleties: You sit “on” it: עַל הַסַּפָּה.

override.N;SG;DEF;PFX: the definite form after the fused prepositions בַּ / לַ (בְּ / לְ + הַ), which drop the ה of the article: הַמְּקָרֵר → (בַּ / לַ)מְּקָרֵר; Wiktionary lists only the full definite form הַמְּקָרֵר.
override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses מְקָרֵר as “refrigerator” — the course concept “fridge”.

profile.feeling: Cold drinks in the summer heat.

examples.tr: The milk is in the fridge.
The fridge is next to the door.
There is nothing in the fridge.

etymology.text: Wiktionary gives no etymology; it is the piʿel present form “cooling”, from the root ק־ר־ר of קַר “cold”.

funFacts: Same root as קַר “cold” and קָרִיר “cool”.
pitfalls: With the article the מ doubles: הַמְּקָרֵר; “in the fridge” = בַּמְּקָרֵר.
Plural מְקָרְרִים.
subtleties: Like German Kühlschrank (“cooling cupboard”), it names the machine by what it does.
